title: India Doubled Gold Tariffs to Save the Rupee — Now Smugglers Are Filling the Gap
excerpt: A tariff hike from 6% to 15% was meant to staunch an $84 billion gold import bill. Instead, grey-market inflows could hit 100 tons this year, jewellers are pivoting to lighter designs, and NRIs heading home for weddings face painfully higher costs.
body:
In May 2026, India more than doubled its import tariff on gold — from 6 percent to 15 percent — in a move aimed squarely at plugging a gaping hole in its balance of payments. The country had spent a record $84 billion on gold and silver imports in the fiscal year to March, nearly a tenth of its total foreign exchange reserves. Those reserves had slipped from $728.49 billion to $690 billion in just ten weeks, pushed down by the Iran war's disruption to oil trade and capital outflows.

The tariff hike was emergency balance-of-payments management. The result, barely a month in, is a textbook case of unintended consequences.

## The Grey Market Roars Back

According to Reuters, citing six separate bullion dealers, grey-market gold imports could exceed 100 metric tons in 2026. At current prices, that represents roughly $14.35 billion worth of gold flowing through unofficial channels — and approximately $2.65 billion in lost tariffs and sales tax.

The economics are brutally simple. Legitimate importers must pay 18.45 percent in combined import duties and goods and services tax. Smugglers pay none of it, enabling them to offer discounts of more than $200 per ounce — or over 4 percent — on official domestic prices. No legal importer can match even a $10 discount, let alone one that runs into three digits.

"There's a margin of more than 2.5 million rupees on bringing in a one-kilo bar, which is roughly the size of an iPhone," a Mumbai-based bullion dealer told Reuters. "It is natural that people will try to make quick bucks."

The numbers track with history. Unofficial gold imports had fallen sharply after India cut tariffs in 2024, dropping from 156 tons in 2023 to 69 tons in 2024 and just 20 tons in 2025. The May 2026 hike has reversed that trend almost overnight.

## Wedding Season Sticker Shock

The tariff increase has landed at the worst possible time, colliding with India's peak wedding and festival season. "Importing ₹1 lakh worth of gold now attracts ₹15,000 in duty, up from ₹6,000 overnight," Prithviraj Kothari, President of the India Bullion and Jewellers Association (IBJA) and Managing Director of RiddiSiddhi Bullions, told Invezz.

The impact is rippling through the jewellery trade. In Ahmedabad, jewellers report that customers who earlier bought 8–10 gram pieces are now opting for lighter designs to stay within budget. Old gold exchange — where buyers trade in existing jewellery for new designs, paying only for the making charges and any additional weight — now accounts for over 40 percent of some retailers' sales.

"Indian gold buying is culturally deep-rooted and not easily deferred," said Varghese Alukkas, Managing Director of Jos Alukkas. But even deep roots bend under pressure: retail buying volumes have dropped, and festive purchases are being deferred where possible.

The Gem and Jewellery Export Promotion Council (GJEPC) has warned that exporters are already struggling with tighter working capital. Bank guarantees for duty-free gold used in jewellery manufacturing have climbed to ₹28–30 lakh per kilogram, straining liquidity for the MSMEs that form the backbone of the sector.

## Why the Government Acted

The rationale behind the tariff hike is not frivolous. India imports nearly all of its domestic gold demand. In a year when oil prices surged due to the Iran–US conflict and the rupee came under sustained pressure, the gold import bill became a macroeconomic liability.

Precious metals imports pushed India's current account deficit wider and weakened the rupee — which, in turn, made oil imports more expensive, creating a feedback loop that the Reserve Bank of India needed to break. Raising gold tariffs was one of the few levers available to policymakers that did not require legislative action.

The RBI has simultaneously been buying gold for its own reserves — India held 822 tons at March-end — and has taken measures to support the rupee, including allowing banks to lend against foreign-currency non-resident deposits.

## What It Means for NRIs

For NRIs planning travel home for weddings or festivals, the math has changed. Gold jewellery prices are up roughly 10 percent since the tariff hike, on top of already record-high international gold prices. A standard bridal set that cost ₹8 lakh a year ago could now approach ₹10 lakh or more.

There are a few practical considerations:

**Duty-free allowances remain in place** — male passengers returning from abroad can carry up to 20 grams of gold (worth up to ₹50,000), and female passengers up to 40 grams (worth up to ₹1 lakh), without paying duty. Beyond that, the full 15 percent duty applies.

**Sovereign Gold Bonds (SGBs)** offer NRIs exposure to gold prices without the import duty or making charges. SGBs are issued by the RBI, carry a 2.5 percent annual interest rate, and are exempt from capital gains tax if held to maturity. They can be purchased through Indian bank accounts, including NRE and NRO accounts.

**Gold ETFs** in India, while they saw net outflows of ₹725 crore in May as investors booked profits, remain a liquid alternative to physical gold for NRIs with demat accounts.

The IBJA and jewellery trade bodies have urged the government to consider reviving the gold monetisation scheme, which would allow households to deposit idle gold with banks and earn interest — potentially mobilising part of India's estimated 25,000 tons of household gold and reducing the need for imports.

## The Bigger Picture

India's gold tariff dilemma is a recurring one. Every government has tried to curb gold demand through duties, and every significant hike has eventually spurred smuggling that erodes the very revenues it was meant to protect. The 2013 tariff hike to 10 percent sent unofficial imports soaring past 150 tons annually. The 2024 cut to 6 percent killed the grey market almost overnight.

Now the cycle has restarted. Whether the government holds at 15 percent through the upcoming budget session or cuts back remains one of the more consequential policy calls for India's external accounts — and for the millions of families, both in India and across the diaspora, for whom gold is not a luxury but a financial and cultural necessity.
